extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, experimental scientists, and students of scientific method (investigators of nature following Baconian induction)
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural method for discovering the 'form' (law) of a natural phenomenon by systematic collection of instances, exclusion of alternatives, and experimental verification; illustrated here for the form of heat. Emphasizes tables of instances, solitary/coruscating examples, method-of-differences, and staged interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct tables of instances (review/presence/absence/degrees)
rubrics_metrics.description: Collect and present a comprehensive review of instances in organized 'tables' (instances where the nature is present, where absent, and of degrees), so the understanding may examine commonalities and differences prior to interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'office and use of these three tables' is to present instances to the understanding; e.g., Table of Degrees of Cold, tables of review. Include many and varied instances, occasionally noting doubtful authority, and repeatedly append 'Let the experiment be tried—Let further inquiry be made.' Use these tables as the empirical foundation before attempting affirmative theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the Exclusive (Rejection) Table to eliminate candidate natures
rubrics_metrics.description: Form hypotheses by negative exclusion: list candidate natures (causes/explanations) and reject those contradicted by instances in the review tables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single contradictory instance destroys a hypothesis; the exclusive table lays foundations for induction. Examples given for heat: reject 'elementary (terrestrial) nature' on account of sun's rays; reject 'celestial nature' on account of subterranean fires; reject 'rarity' on account of ignited metals; reject 'flame or light' on account of boiling water and air. Repeat and expand the exclusive table until only the residuum remains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attempt affirmative interpretation only after constructing and weighing the tables ('First vintage')
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not hastily posit positive forms; first prepare review and exclusive tables, then grant the 'liberty of the understanding' to attempt the first affirmative interpretation (the 'first vintage').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'liberty of the understanding' or 'first vintage' is the commencement of interpretation after exhaustive collection and rejection. This staged approach prevents premature 'phantoms' and ill-defined axioms; affirmative forms should arise as the residuum after correct exclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use solitary and conspicuous (prerogative / coruscating) instances
rubrics_metrics.description: Prioritize solitary, conspicuous, or coruscatory instances that isolate the nature under inquiry by sharing nothing in common with other subjects except the nature in question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solitary instances accelerate and confirm exclusion (a few may be as valuable as many). Examples: prisms, crystalline gems, dews, distinct veins in marble, variegated spots in flowers—these isolate 'color' from other properties. Seek instances where the form is 'unembarrassed' by other natures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlation criterion for identifying a form
rubrics_metrics.description: A candidate form must be (a) always present when the phenomenon is present, (b) absent when it is absent, and (c) increase and decrease with the phenomenon—i.e., correlate across presence/absence and degrees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On individual review of instances, find a nature 'always to be present and absent with the given nature, to increase and decrease with it.' Use presence/absence tables and degrees to test correlation before accepting a form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish form (law) from transitive effect or common notion
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not confuse the form (the law or native constitution of a thing) with transitive or communicative phenomena (e.g., 'heating' vs. 'heat') or with vulgar/compound notions like 'fire.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: heating (the process by which a body grows warm at approach of a hot body) is not the form of heat and must be excluded from the form. The notion of 'fire' is vulgar (a conjunction of heat and light) and of no assistance to discovering the true form; aim to find the simple law of action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of genus and specific differences (identify genus then limiting differences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Find the general genus that unites instances and then determine the specific differences that limit that genus into the precise form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For heat the genus is 'motion' and Bacon lists four differences that limit it into the form of heat: (I) expansive motion (striving to dilate); (II) tendency upward (expansion bearing the body upward); (III) motion of the small particles restrained and alternating (not uniform bulk motion); (IV) rapid, non-sluggish stimulating motion in particles of tolerable dimension. Use experiments (e.g., tongs/poker in fire, distillations per descensum, thermometers, compression extinguishing tinder) to test each difference.

rubrics_metrics.name: A single contradictory instance suffices to refute a proposed form
rubrics_metrics.description: Any single contradictory instance in the tables destroys the hypothesis that a given nature is the form of the phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The exclusive table demonstrates that 'every contradictory instance destroys a hypothesis.' Thus, seek and record contrary instances carefully; do not require many counterexamples—one is decisive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize experiment and empirical trial ('Let the experiment be tried')
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeatedly test hypotheses and suggested differences by concrete experiments; wherever the text says 'Let the experiment be tried—Let further inquiry be made,' follow with controlled trials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested experimental probes include: burning-glass distance experiments, thermometer construction (glass tube with water), burying substances in dung to test latent heat, compression of burning tinder to extinguish flame, using bellows/blowpipe to show motion increases heat, and comparative heating of rods/tubes to test upward tendency of heat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use degrees and comparative ordering to refine understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare degrees of the phenomenon across different substances and contexts (animals, flames, ignited bodies, heavenly bodies) to build an ordered scale and reveal regularities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: rank flames and ignited substances (spirits of wine, straw, wood, oil, pitch, sulphur, gunpowder), compare animal heats (insects vs. quadrupeds vs. birds), observe planetary and stellar variations, and test how distance/focus (burning-glass) or motion (bellows) affect effect-strength. Degree comparisons inform exclusion and the search for limiting differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan induction with supports, corrections, variations, prerogative ordering, limits, and applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Induction is not a single act but a process requiring supports for induction, methods for correction, adapting investigation by subject, selecting prerogative natures for first/last study, defining limits of inquiry, preparing for investigation, and establishing ascending/descending axioms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As listed in the text (XXI): 1) prerogative instances; 2) supports of induction; 3) correction of induction; 4) vary investigation according to subject; 5) prerogative natures for investigation order; 6) limits of investigation; 7) application to practical purposes; 8) preparations for investigation; 9) ascending/descending scale of axioms. Treat induction as a staged, corrective, and adaptive methodology rather than an immediate inference.
